newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rwandan refugees begin arriving in Congo - UNHCR.
newsitem.headline: Rwandan refugees begin arriving in Congo - UNHCR.

text.p: Hundreds of Rwandan Hutu refugees have made their way almost 1,500 km (900 miles) across the breadth of Zaire and have begun appearing in the Congo, United Nations officials said on Sunday.
Peter Kessler, spokesman for the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR said 50 refugees had been seen by aid officials at Loukolela, about 350 kms (200 miles) north east of Brazzaville.
He said a western missionary at Liranga, about 50 kms (30 miles) further east, had reported over 2,600 refugee arrivals in the past few days.
"We had a team confirm the Loukolela arrivals and hope to do the same for Liranga in the next day or so," Kessler told Reuters.
Loukolela, situated on the swampy convergence of the Zaire and Ubangui rivers, lies opposite the similarly named Zairean town of Lukolela.
To have reached this point, the refugees have cut through what is considered some of the most dense forest on earth and traversed scores of rivers in their eight-month trek.

The refugees were among more than 300,000 who fled west in October from their camps on the Zaire-Rwanda border rather than join more than a million other Hutu refugees who returned home when Zairean rebels began an offensive that has taken them virtually to Kinshasha.
The refugees originally fled Rwanda in 1994 to escape reprisals for any role they might have been suspected of in the genocide of over 800,000 Rwandan Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
Meanwhile scores of refugees on Sunday began arriving at Biaro Camp, about 41 kms (25 miles) south of Kisangani, in the hope of joining a U.N. airlift back to Rwanda.
The new arrivals said they had walked from Ubundu, more than 100 kms (65 miles) further south, after hearing the airlift had finally got underway.
Many were in pitiful condition and gorged on dry corn flour offered to them by fellow refugees already in the camp.
One man, his foot broken from what he said was an attack by Zairean villagers, had limped almost the whole way while carrying his daughter.
The U.N. airlift continued on Sunday with nearly 2,000 more flying home, bringing the total since it began on April 27 to more than 18,000.

U.N. officials hope to complete an airlift of the remaining 25,000 refugees at Biaro camp within 10 days, but are at odds with rebel authorities over how many more may remain hidden in the forests of eastern Zaire.
Aid organisations believe more than 200,000 refugees are still unaccounted for, but Rwandan officials insist that around 55,000 remain.
